On 60 previously unseen QASPER training-split articles (188 questions, 169 evidence-evaluable), the policy triggers hybrid retrieval on 46 questions (24.5\%) and obtains the same evidence Hit@10 as always-hybrid retrieval (78.70\%, versus 76.92\% for always-keep). Paired, paper-cluster bootstrap intervals do not establish a reliable utility advantage. We further compare generated answers from a 4-bit Qwen3-4B model under the three retrieval policies. Provisional answer-level assessments show no clear correctness or faithfulness improvement after partial review, despite the evidence-retrieval result. The generation assessments remain model-assisted and lack independent human validation. These results expose an important distinction between retrieving relevant evidence efficiently and improving the reliability of the generated answer. The work is presented as a reproducible empirical study, not a claim of statistically established answer-quality superiority.
title: When Is Additional Retrieval Worthwhile? A Cost-Aware Study of Evidence Gain and Answer Reliability in RAG

summary: Training-time explanation regularization is often evaluated by whether saliency maps become more concentrated within annotated regions. We argue that this criterion alone is insufficient: transformation consistency, lesion localization, and faithfulness to the classifier are distinct properties and should be evaluated separately, particularly in medical imaging. We examine this distinction through a case study of Contrastive Grad-CAM Consistency (CGC) in three-class brain tumor MRI classification. Using a single-channel ResNet-50 with five-fold patient-grouped cross-validation, we compare a cross-entropy baseline with CGC. CGC changes overall Pointing Game (PG) from $27.24\%$ to $36.02\%$ and Relevance Mass Accuracy (RMA) from $11.17\%$ to $18.01\%$, while classification accuracy changes from $93.63\%$ to $94.87\%$. Perturbation-based faithfulness metrics show inconsistent changes: Insertion Area Under the Curve (IAUC) changes from $0.73$ to $0.78$, whereas Deletion Area Under the Curve (DAUC) favors the baseline ($0.36$ versus $0.41$; lower is better), and overall Iterative Removal Of Features (IROF) is $0.57$ for both models. These results support our position that improved spatial agreement with pathology should not be interpreted as a general improvement in explanation faithfulness. We therefore recommend property-specific evaluation in which the property targeted by the explanation objective, spatial agreement with reference regions, and model reliance are measured and reported separately.
title: Localization Gains from Explanation Regularization Should Not Be Interpreted as Faithfulness Gains.

summary: The study examines the physiological adaptation of boxers to mid-altitude conditions (1,800‒2,200 m above sea level) and substantiates the need to individualize training loads based on functional markers: blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), heart rate (HR), lactate levels, and maximum oxygen consumption (VO2). The article presents the results of a pedagogical experiment involving 24 qualified boxers (CMS and MS), divided into control and experimental groups. The experimental methodology included real-time monitoring of functional markers and real-time adjustment of the weekly microcycle. Following a 4-week high-altitude training camp, the experimental group demonstrated a significant increase in VO2 by 6.8%, hemoglobin concentration by 4.3%, and an improvement in the heart rate recovery index by 34.4% compared to the control group (p<0.05). The obtained data demonstrate the high efficiency of an individualized approach to load planning in midaltitude areas and are recommended for use in the training of highly qualified athletes.
title: Individualization of Boxing Training Loads in Middle-Altitude Conditions Based on Functional Adaptation Markers.

summary: Presents the results of an experimental study on the effectiveness of computer biomechanical analysis in improving the technical training of qualified wrestlers. The aim of the study was to determine the effect of an integrated biomechanical throw-assessment system on athletes' competitive performance. Thirty-two wrestlers (Masters of Sport and Candidates for Master of Sport) participated in the pedagogical experiment and were divided into a control group (n=16) and an experimental group (n=16). The experiment lasted six months. The control group trained according to the standard programme, while the experimental group additionally used a hardware-software complex for three-dimensional biomechanical motion analysis based on inertial sensors and computer video modelling. Kinematic and dynamic parameters of the key throw elements were recorded: joint angular velocities, trajectory of the overall centre of mass, and the temporal force-transfer profile. As a result of the experimental methodology, athletes in the experimental group showed a significant improvement in biomechanical movement coordination (p<0.05); the effectiveness of technical actions in competitions increased: the throw execution rate rose from 38.4% to 56.7%, and the judges' technical score from 6.1 to 7.8 points. It was established that systematic feedback through computer biomechanical data forms a more stable motor stereotype and accelerates the correction of technical errors. The data obtained confirm the feasibility of introducing computer biomechanical technologies into the training system for qualified wrestlers.
title: Effectiveness of Computerized Biomechanical Assessment of Throwing Technique in Qualified Wrestlers

summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Methodology : Uses lattice regularisation, renormalisation-group control of the continuum limit, and Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction of a relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski space. Expresses the clustering rate of the reflection-positive two-point function as the mass gap. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). Key Innovations & Structure : Works in the flow-time coordinate where the dimensional-transmutation scale is an entire function and the marginal coupling region is compact. Proves the factorisation of the clustering rate and demonstrates that the mass gap equals the spectral gap of the transfer operator restricted to the centre-charged sector. Verifies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms (temperedness, reflection positivity, symmetry) conditional on identified inputs (uniform non-percolation, rotational invariance restoration, and limit uniqueness). Closes with a closure scheme, dimensional calibration against three-dimensional models, and explicit worked examples. The monograph titled "The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional $SU(N)$ Yang–Mills Theory" presents a construction of pure quantum Yang–Mills theory with a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional Euclidean space. Its primary objective is to establish the existence of the theory and the strict positivity of its mass gap , reducing the overall problem to a small set of explicitly identified, non-analytic inputs.
title: When is 4D-Yang-Mills-Theorie possible; The Mass Gap of Four-Dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills Theory: A Construction, Its Reduction to a Single Non-Analytic Input, and a Scheme for Its Closure

summary: As spectroscopic surveys grow, estimating galaxy properties such as metallicity, star formation rate, and redshift becomes computationally cumbersome. Methods of estimating such properties rely on template spectra or curated redshift catalogs, which fail to represent the diversity of objects seen in large-scale surveys. We present UnEZ, a fully unsupervised, physics-informed machine learning model that can predict spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths with no prior redshift or line strength labels. An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes/widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a unique template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve, and spectral model. UnEZ was tested on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 18 due to its large dataset and thoroughly vetted redshift catalog which serves as an independent benchmark. Despite the lack of templates, line strength labels, or redshift labels, UnEZ's performance competes with modern redshift estimation algorithms. At SNR > 10, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 0.459% and a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of $1.237 \times 10^{-4}$. At SNR > 3, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 3.89% and an NMAD of $1.471 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how UnEZ's line strength and redshift predictions can be utilized for various purposes such as constructing template spectra required in traditional redshift estimation algorithms. UnEZ illustrates how a fully unsupervised neural network can allow redshift, among other galaxy properties, to emerge naturally from the spectra themselves, providing a template-free, label-free approach that scales to the demands of future surveys.
title: UnEZ: A Fully Unsupervised Self-Templating Neural Network for Redshift and Line Strength Estimation

summary: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.
title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions

summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.
title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution

summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Generated suites almost always execute, but discrimination lags behind: the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval, so executability alone overstates test quality. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. QTestBench offers a reproducible, cross-framework benchmark for the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.
title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code

summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for graph understanding and decision-making, while System One models such as Jev select directly from supplied options. However, the capabilities of System One models on graph-related tasks remain unclear. We introduce GraphDecisionBench, a model-independent benchmark that combines structural task profiles, matched graph-text input contrasts and heuristic-proposal controls to diagnose graph decision performance. We evaluate Jev and related choice-based models alongside language-model baselines, covering fourteen model-interface configurations. Jev's results illustrate the benchmark's central distinctions: accurate adjacency recognition does not guarantee broader structural correctness, joint graph-text input does not consistently improve prediction, and feasible construction does not establish high solution quality. Its task contracts, candidate interfaces and scoring rules support comparison across native selectors and language-model adapters. Code and aggregate results are available at https://github.com/VictorYXL/GraphDecisionBench.
title: GraphDecisionBench: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks

summary: We develop a price-based framework for stochastic portfolio theory in which trading strategies are generated from nominal price weights and evaluated relative to a price-weighted benchmark. Stock splits and reverse splits induce jumps in the generating weights without changing the value of existing investments. In a semimartingale market with predictable adjustment events, we incorporate the corresponding share adjustments into the self-financing condition and construct additively and multiplicatively generated strategies with explicit jump-corrected wealth decompositions. For additive generation, an entropy-based example exhibits relative wealth tending to $-\infty$ almost surely under repeated splits, demonstrating why the usual argument for long-horizon relative arbitrage does not extend directly. We also show that advance adjustment information alone provides no model-free guarantee of improved performance for functionally generated portfolios. For multiplicative generation, wealth-preserving restarts retain the classical portfolio allocation evaluated at the current price weights. We also establish a correspondence with the capitalization-based framework that preserves absolute wealth and yields a strategy-independent benchmark conversion. We illustrate the framework using daily NYSE data, comparing price- and capitalization-weighted benchmarks and the corresponding diversity-weighted portfolios across price- and capitalization-selected universes.
title: A Price-Based Framework for Stochastic Portfolio Theory

summary: We develop a price-based framework for stochastic portfolio theory in which trading strategies are generated from nominal price weights and evaluated relative to a price-weighted benchmark. Stock splits and reverse splits induce jumps in the generating weights without changing the value of existing investments. In a semimartingale market with predictable adjustment events, we incorporate the corresponding share adjustments into the self-financing condition and construct additively and multiplicatively generated strategies with explicit jump-corrected wealth decompositions. For additive generation, an entropy-based example exhibits relative wealth tending to $-\infty$ almost surely under repeated splits, demonstrating why the usual argument for long-horizon relative arbitrage does not extend directly. We also show that advance adjustment information alone provides no model-free guarantee of improved performance for functionally generated portfolios. For multiplicative generation, wealth-preserving restarts retain the classical portfolio allocation evaluated at the current price weights. We also establish a correspondence with the capitalization-based framework that preserves absolute wealth and yields a strategy-independent benchmark conversion. We illustrate the framework using daily NYSE data, comparing price- and capitalization-weighted benchmarks and the corresponding diversity-weighted portfolios across price- and capitalization-selected universes.
title: A Price-Based Framework for Stochastic Portfolio Theory

summary: We present a systematic study of the quantum phase transition from a Dirac semimetal to an antiferromagnetic Mott insulator in the honeycomb-lattice Hubbard model, using finite-temperature auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) simulations. Given the dynamical critical exponent $z=1$ at criticality, we scale the inverse temperature $β$ with the linear system size $L$, i.e., $βt=L$ (with $t$ as the hopping amplitude), to approach the thermodynamic and zero-temperature limits simultaneously. On the algorithmic front, we generalize the fast Fourier transform in path propagation to multi-sublattice systems and employ the delayed update technique in configuration updates to accelerate the AFQMC simulations. These advances enable us to access unprecedented system sizes of up to $3528$ sites (with $L=42$ and $βt = 42$). We additionally use twist-averaged boundary conditions to reduce the finite-size effects in computed observables. On the physical side, we determine the Dirac quantum criticality via finite-size scaling analysis of the spin correlations and off-diagonal single-particle Green's function, and locate the critical point at $U_c/t=3.731(4)$ with the critical exponents $ν=1.097(7)$, $η_φ=0.72(2)$ and $η_ψ=0.155(6)$. We further corroborate the critical point by examining several relevant quantities, including the quasiparticle weight, Fermi-liquid parameter, charge compressibility, $U$-derivative of double occupancy, and fidelity susceptibility. Our work establishes an independent benchmark for the chiral Heisenberg Gross-Neveu-Yukawa criticality in the honeycomb Hubbard model, offering a complementary perspective to previous ground-state simulations.
title: Finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo study of Dirac quantum criticality: Algorithmic advances and comprehensive analysis

summary: Many existing Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions on mobile devices rely on an extensive collection of sensitive data, raising privacy concerns and often requiring storage for both context and model improvement. Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) aims to address this by emphasizing mobile device integration and a privacy-first design. The central claim of PCC is that it does not store any user data and that user input and user accounts are unlinkable. While most of the PCC system specifications are public, compiled binaries add a layer of opaqueness. There are no reproducible builds, and there are no symbols within those binaries, creating potential discrepancies between the specification and what is shipped to the user. Additionally, the underlying models and interfaces for querying PCC are not openly accessible, limiting academic evaluation of model properties, such as accuracy. This poses a challenge in assessing whether a privacy-preserving approach like PCC is actually trustworthy while also providing high-quality answers. We are the first to reverse-engineer the PCC implementation on mobile devices to evaluate privacy aspects and to open its non-public interfaces on local devices to support custom PCC queries. We demonstrate this level of access beyond Apple's intended use cases by independently benchmarking the PCC model. We enable future research by making our PCC benchmarking framework publicly available.
title: Unlocking Apple's Private Cloud Compute: An Analysis of Privacy-Preserving Artificial Intelligence

summary: This paper presents our submission to the ACMMM25 - Grand Challenge on Multimedia Verification. We developed a multi-agent verification system that combines Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with specialized verification tools to detect multimedia misinformation. Our system operates through six stages: raw data processing, planning, information extraction, deep research, evidence collection, and report generation. The core Deep Researcher Agent employs four tools: reverse image search, metadata analysis, fact-checking databases, and verified news processing that extracts spatial, temporal, attribution, and motivational context. We demonstrate our approach on a challenge dataset sample involving complex multimedia content. Our system successfully verified content authenticity, extracted precise geolocation and timing information, and traced source attribution across multiple platforms, effectively addressing real-world multimedia verification scenarios.
title: Multimedia Verification Through Multi-Agent Deep Research Multimodal Large Language Models

summary: We develop and validate a one-dimensional electron-ion two-fluid model, self-consistently coupled to Maxwell equations, for magnetosonic structures generated by a moving charged source. The model is independently benchmarked against kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations to assess its ability to reproduce electrostatic and electromagnetic responses. In the zero-magnetic-field limit, the electrostatic precursor structures are validated using the Korteweg--de Vries amplitude--width invariant. For a finite magnetic field, the frequency and propagation speed of the far wake are consistent with the low-frequency fast-magnetosonic branch, providing a linear benchmark for the electromagnetic response. The model reproduces the transition from a wake-dominated regime to localized forward precursors as the source velocity exceeds the magnetosonic speed, and to source-locked pinned structures at higher velocities. Independent PIC simulations recover the principal features of these regimes, supporting the validity of the two-fluid description for the parameters considered. By retaining separate electron and ion dynamics, electron inertia, and charge-separation effects, the validated model provides a framework for investigating source-driven plasma-wave structures across a broader range of plasma conditions and source-magnetic-field geometries, with potential applications to interpreting plasma-wave signatures associated with moving charged objects in space plasmas.
title: Magnetosonic Solitons Driven by a Moving Charged Source: Two-Fluid Modeling and PIC Validation

summary: This version extends the previously archived replication package for within-project and cross-project just-in-time software defect prediction. The package includes four additional experimental components: C4: Controlled training-set size and class-distribution matching across 13 Apache projects, four machine learning algorithms, and 20 model refits. C5: Sensitivity analyses examining SHAP evaluation sample size and background selection. C6: A descriptive simulation of defect-oriented commit review prioritization. C7: External validation using six historical Kamei projects, comprising 960 model records and corresponding global SHAP feature-importance vectors. The C7 source-provenance audit confirmed that SHA-256 fingerprints, input summaries, and temporal training/test splits matched the archived experimental records for all six projects. All 36 crosschecks passed. This verification does not constitute independent retraining of all models. The findings concern the sensitivity of global SHAP feature rankings to training conditions. They do not establish causal effects, explanation correctness, or demonstrated benefits to software developers. The archive contains experimental outputs, analysis scripts, figures, and reproducibility documentation. Original third-party ApacheJIT and Kamei datasets are not redistributed. Previous version: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23301636
title: Replication Package for Training-Source Sensitivity of Global SHAP Explanations in Just-in-Time Defect Prediction: Matched-Class Refits and Kamei External Validation

summary: Supporting code and data for the exploratory ETV4 case study “Sequence and family context shape ETV4 representations in protein language models”. The deposit contains 711 biological/control activation arrays from ESM-2 650M, ESM-2 3B and ProFam, 71 numerical-qualification arrays with receipts, and a versioned repository snapshot containing processed results, input sequences and prompts, fixed readout masks and configurations, analysis and figure-generation code, provenance and supplementary information. A portable NumPy analysis verifies array identities and recomputes both canonical summaries without rerunning the protein models. All saved fields, including 107,102 numerical values, matched in local verification. The study examines dependence of protein representations on sequence and family context; it does not establish regulatory specificity or an allosteric mechanism. Original code is licensed under MIT; original derived data and written materials are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party materials retain their own terms. The code snapshot filename identifies its Git commit. Development repository: https://github.com/amoyag/etv4-context-representations .

summary: We present the first mechanised formalisation of Romanov's Triplet Logic (TLS) in the Rocq proof assistant. TLS is a combinatorial framework originally motivated by Boolean satisfiability, based on triplet structures and a filter that we call Simple Vertex Intersection (SVI). We formalise the core of TLS, including its translation from 3-CNF, the clearing procedure, and the SVI algorithm. For the well-formed sliding-window fragment, we prove explicit polynomial-time bounds for the filter stages and verify the translation and intersection operations. Our main contribution is a precise correctness boundary: for general formulas, SVI non-emptiness is necessary but not sufficient for satisfiability; for aligned structures, we prove a full bi-implication, extended to systems of structures. We also formalise the grouped-window translation and provide a formal counterexample to its completeness. We introduce VFR (Verified Filter for Romanov's triplet logic), an extracted OCaml prototype that implements a verified decision procedure for the sliding-window fragment and a sound filter for general 3-CNF, with a Python runtime and Docker packaging. Benchmarks corroborate the predicted behaviour, and the complete toolchain is available as a curated Zenodo artifact. The Rocq development comprises over 23,000 lines of code, with 424 proved lemmas and no unproved assumptions.
title: Formal Verification of Romanov's Triplet Logic: A Verified Filter for Sliding-window 3-CNF with Application to Structured Formulas

summary: We present JOR-Bench, a collection of five Japanese-language benchmarks for evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to formulate and solve operations research (OR) problems. Each benchmark is a Japanese translation of an existing English benchmark: IndustryOR, MAMO Complex LP, NL4OPT, OptiBench, and OptMATH, covering 1,319 problems spanning linear programming, mixed-integer programming, non-linear programming, and combinatorial optimization. JOR-Bench is a solver-independent benchmark that can be used with any solver or programming language, and consists of pairs of Japanese problem statements and expected numerical answers. We evaluate seven LLMs, including multilingual general-purpose models and Japanese-specialized models, on both the original English and the new Japanese versions, and compare performance across languages. For the main evaluation, we standardize execution with the Python interface to OR-Tools to make model outputs comparable and reproducible with open-source software. Our results show that OR formulation ability is largely language-neutral for strong multilingual models; the overall average accuracy difference between English and Japanese is only $-0.3$ pp. Yet error analysis reveals subtle cross-lingual differences, including a pragmatic disambiguation failure in some domains that causes models to output decision-variable values instead of the objective value when the prompt is in Japanese.

summary: Reusable robot skills are becoming the basic units through which embodied agents turn open-ended instructions into long-horizon physical behavior. We argue that, while foundation models have collapsed the cost of creating these skills, the cost of trusting them has not. Existing skill-evolution loops refine skills through execution feedback, unit tests, environment reward, or LLM self-critique, but these signals provide only trace-level evidence: they show that a skill worked on sampled executions, not that skill-induced plans satisfy temporal safety contracts under untested conditions. We introduce VASO, a framework for verification-guided self-evolution of LLM-generated robot skill contracts. In VASO, each skill is represented as a semantic contract with two coupled interfaces: a formal interface that aligns robot states, observations, and control commands with logical propositions for model checking, and a planner-facing interface that guides executable behavior generation. A model checker first filters logically inconsistent skill contracts, then verifies plans induced by the skill against global and local temporal specifications. When verification fails, VASO translates the counterexample trace into a textual gradient that updates the reusable skill contract while keeping foundation-model weights frozen. On Clearpath Jackal and PX4 quadcopter tasks, VASO reaches 97.2% formal-specification compliance using fewer than 100 optimization samples, outperforming execution-feedback, prompt-optimization, and fine-tuning baselines. To our knowledge, VASO is the first framework that closes the loop between formal verification and self-evolving LLM-generated skills for physical AI agents: formal counterexamples become optimization feedback for reusable robot skill contracts, rather than merely verifying one-off plans, tuning planner prompts, or fine-tuning model weights.
title: VASO: Formally Verifiable Self-Evolving Skills for Physical AI Agents

summary: Mathematical reasoning demands two critical, complementary skills: constructing rigorous proofs for true statements and discovering counterexamples that disprove false ones. However, current AI efforts in mathematics focus almost exclusively on proof construction, often neglecting the equally important task of finding counterexamples. In this paper, we address this gap by fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to reason about and generate counterexamples. We formalize this task as formal counterexample generation, which requires LLMs not only to propose candidate counterexamples but also to produce formal proofs that can be automatically verified in the Lean 4 theorem prover. To enable effective learning, we introduce a symbolic mutation strategy that constructs candidate counterexample-generation tasks by systematically extracting theorems and removing selected hypotheses. Together with curated datasets, this strategy enables a multi-reward expert iteration framework that substantially enhances both the effectiveness and efficiency of training LLMs for counterexample generation and theorem proving. Experiments on three newly collected benchmarks validate the advantages of our approach, showing that the mutation strategy and training framework yield substantial performance gains.
title: Learning to Disprove: Formal Counterexample Generation with Large Language Models

summary: Hydrogen threatens the structural integrity of metals and thus predicting hydrogen-material interactions is key to unlocking the role of hydrogen in the energy transition. Quantifying the interplay between material deformation and hydrogen diffusion ahead of cracks and other stress concentrators is key to the prediction and prevention of hydrogen-assisted failures. In this work, a generalised theoretical and computational framework is presented that for the first time encompasses: (i) stress-assisted diffusion, (ii) hydrogen trapping due to multiple trap types, rigorously accounting for the rate of creation of dislocation trap sites, (iii) hydrogen transport through dislocations, (iv) equilibrium (Oriani) and non-equilibrium (McNabb-Foster) trapping kinetics, (v) hydrogen-induced softening, and (vi) hydrogen uptake, considering the role of hydrostatic stresses and local electrochemistry. Particular emphasis is placed on the numerical implementation in COMSOL Multiphysics, releasing the relevant models and discussing stability, discretisation and solver details. Each of the elements of the framework is independently benchmarked against results from the literature and implications for the prediction of hydrogen-assisted fractures are discussed. The second part of this work (Part II) shows how these crack tip predictions can be combined with crack growth simulations.
title: A COMSOL framework for predicting hydrogen embrittlement -- Part I: coupled hydrogen transport

summary: We study the performance of sequential contention resolution and matching algorithms on random graphs with vanishing edge probabilities. When the edges of the graph are processed in an adversarially-chosen order, we derive a new OCRS that is $0.382$-selectable, attaining the "independence benchmark" from the literature under the vanishing edge probabilities assumption. Complementary to this positive result, we show that no OCRS can be more than $0.390$-selectable, significantly improving upon the upper bound of $0.428$ from the literature. We also derive negative results that are specialized to bipartite graphs or subfamilies of OCRSs. Meanwhile, when the edges of the graph are processed in a uniformly random order, we show that the simple greedy contention resolution scheme which accepts all active and feasible edges is $1/2$-selectable. This result is tight due to a known upper bound. We then show that when the algorithm can choose the processing order, a slight tweak to the random order---give each vertex a random priority and process edges in lexicographic order---results in a strictly better contention resolution scheme that is $1-\ln(2-1/e)\approx0.510$-selectable. Moreover, we show that this bound is tight over any sequential contention resolution scheme, even one which may adaptively choose the order in which it processes edges. This provides a separation from the $0.544$ upper bound for offline contention resolution implied by the classic result of Karp and Sipser. Our positive results also apply to online matching on $1$-uniform random graphs with vanishing (non-identical) edge probabilities, extending and unifying some results from the random graphs literature.
title: Online Matching and Contention Resolution for Edge Arrivals with Vanishing Probabilities

summary: We introduce an automated, formal, counterexample-based approach to synthesise Barrier Certificates (BC) for the safety verification of continuous and hybrid dynamical models. The approach is underpinned by an inductive framework: this is structured as a sequential loop between a learner, which manipulates a candidate BC structured as a neural network, and a sound verifier, which either certifies the candidate's validity or generates counter-examples to further guide the learner. We compare the approach against state-of-the-art techniques, over polynomial and non-polynomial dynamical models: the outcomes show that we can synthesise sound BCs up to two orders of magnitude faster, with in particular a stark speedup on the verification engine (up to five orders less), whilst needing a far smaller data set (up to three orders less) for the learning part. Beyond improvements over the state of the art, we further challenge the new approach on a hybrid dynamical model and on larger-dimensional models, and showcase the numerical robustness of our algorithms and codebase.
title: Automated and Formal Synthesis of Neural Barrier Certificates for Dynamical Models

summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 42 examines why enterprise artificial intelligence strategy is moving beyond the assumption that one general-purpose model should serve every workload. The paper argues that model selection is increasingly an intelligence-allocation decision involving capability, cost, latency, governance, data restrictions, decision authority and measurable business outcomes. As enterprise AI expands across routine classification, specialised extraction, complex reasoning, multimodal production and consequential decisions, different categories of work require different execution approaches. The paper distinguishes model selection, inference tiering, model routing, policy-controlled routing and outcome verification. It proposes that enterprises should first determine whether generative inference is required, define the minimum capability needed, apply mandatory eligibility constraints, select an appropriate execution route, establish escalation conditions and verify whether the completed outcome meets a predetermined business acceptance standard. Six author-developed frameworks structure this operating model. The AI Workload Classification framework divides work into deterministic, routine language, specialised, complex reasoning and consequential-decision categories. The Model Routing Matrix separates mandatory policy constraints from economic and performance preferences. The Capability-Cost Frontier evaluates eligible models against verified acceptance and complete delivery cost. The Model Escalation Ladder defines structured movement from deterministic execution through compact, specialised and frontier intelligence to human authority. Minimum Sufficient Intelligence identifies the least expensive eligible intelligence capable of satisfying the complete business requirement. Cost per Accepted Outcome, or CPAO, measures total attributable workflow delivery cost against completed business outcomes that satisfy defined acceptance standards. The analysis also challenges the assumption that sophisticated routing automatically produces superior economics. Evidence from LLMRouterBench shows strong model complementarity while demonstrating that several routing approaches do not consistently outperform simpler baselines. The paper therefore argues that routing complexity requires evidence of incremental value rather than being treated as an architectural objective in itself. Commercial case studies examine three different intelligence-allocation mechanisms. Sword Health illustrates central gateway control, provider portability, policy enforcement and cost attribution. Forethought demonstrates how specialised deployment, multi-model endpoints and serverless inference affect AI infrastructure economics. gimmefy illustrates multimodel execution across different marketing modalities and provider capabilities. The cases are treated separately because their reported outcomes rely on different commercial baselines and measurement approaches. The paper proposes a 90-day evaluation path based on workload classification, baseline measurement, shadow testing, controlled deployment and an explicit investment decision. Leadership measurement should focus on accepted outcome rate, cost per accepted outcome, realised business value, consequential errors, latency distribution, policy compliance, escalation and rework, and model substitution readiness. summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 42 examines why enterprise artificial intelligence strategy is moving beyond the assumption that one general-purpose model should serve every workload. The paper argues that model selection is increasingly an intelligence-allocation decision involving capability, cost, latency, governance, data restrictions, decision authority and measurable business outcomes. As enterprise AI expands across routine classification, specialised extraction, complex reasoning, multimodal production and consequential decisions, different categories of work require different execution approaches. The paper distinguishes model selection, inference tiering, model routing, policy-controlled routing and outcome verification. It proposes that enterprises should first determine whether generative inference is required, define the minimum capability needed, apply mandatory eligibility constraints, select an appropriate execution route, establish escalation conditions and verify whether the completed outcome meets a predetermined business acceptance standard. Six author-developed frameworks structure this operating model. The AI Workload Classification framework divides work into deterministic, routine language, specialised, complex reasoning and consequential-decision categories. The Model Routing Matrix separates mandatory policy constraints from economic and performance preferences. The Capability-Cost Frontier evaluates eligible models against verified acceptance and complete delivery cost. The Model Escalation Ladder defines structured movement from deterministic execution through compact, specialised and frontier intelligence to human authority. Minimum Sufficient Intelligence identifies the least expensive eligible intelligence capable of satisfying the complete business requirement. Cost per Accepted Outcome, or CPAO, measures total attributable workflow delivery cost against completed business outcomes that satisfy defined acceptance standards. summary: Herrero García, José Luis. “La reivindicación marroquí y la soberanía española sobre Ceuta y Melilla.” Boletín CODESEL , vol. 2, no. 11, Oct. 2026, pp. 1–15. ISSN 3045-7750 LEGAL REVIEW The territorial claims advanced by the Kingdom of Morocco concerning Ceuta, Melilla and the remaining Spanish territories in North Africa constitute a particularly complex controversy at the intersection of international public law, historical sovereignty, territorial integrity, decolonisation and European security. Although these claims are frequently presented through the political vocabulary of colonial restitution and national reunification, their historical and legal foundations require examination beyond the geographical proximity of the disputed territories or the nationalist narratives surrounding Morocco's independence. In this extensive historical and juridical study, José Luis Herrero García undertakes a systematic examination of Moroccan territorial revisionism and the legal continuity of Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla. His principal argument challenges the doctrine of Greater Morocco by distinguishing premodern religious allegiances, dynastic dominion and military expansion from the legal characteristics of territorial sovereignty under contemporary international law. Through the combined analysis of medieval political formations, historical treaties, constitutional provisions, international judicial reasoning and European institutional practice, the article develops a comprehensive interpretation of the historical and legal circumstances supporting Spain's position. The significance of the study extends beyond the bilateral dispute, raising fundamental questions concerning the construction of historical territorial titles, the stability of international borders and the limitations imposed by international law upon irredentist claims. The analysis begins with the historical development of Moroccan territorial ambitions, tracing the ideological origins of the Greater Morocco doctrine to nationalist movements that emerged during the first half of the twentieth century and acquired particular prominence around Moroccan independence in 1956. Herrero García identifies the influence of Allal el Fassi and the Istiqlal Party in formulating an expansive conception of Moroccan territorial identity that encompassed not only Ceuta, Melilla and other Spanish possessions, but also Western Sahara, Mauritania, territories in present-day Algeria and parts of the Sahel. This geographical conception was supported by references to the alleged historical boundaries of successive Islamic dynasties and to the religious and political relationships established between Moroccan rulers and neighbouring populations. The author questions the legitimacy of interpreting such relationships as evidence of an uninterrupted historical sovereignty comparable to that exercised by modern States. This criticism is particularly important because the nationalist reconstruction of medieval territorial boundaries disregards the institutional differences between dynastic empires, tribal confederations and the contemporary territorial State. The study therefore distinguishes the historical existence of political influence from the establishment of an internationally recognisable sovereign title, arguing that the territorial expansion of former ruling dynasties cannot automatically generate legal entitlements for the present Moroccan monarchy. One of the article's most substantial contributions is its detailed reconstruction of the Almoravid, Almohad, Marinid and Saadian political formations. The discussion of the Almoravids emphasises their origins among Saharan Berber communities associated with territories situated in present-day Mauritania, thereby questioning the assumption that their subsequent expansion establishes a uniquely Moroccan historical entitlement. summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 43 examines the governance and evidence requirements that arise when artificial intelligence influences consequential business decisions. The paper defines a decision chain of custody as a controlled, verifiable record connecting the information used, systems involved, applicable policies, delegated authority, approvals, execution and preserved evidence behind an AI-influenced decision. Its central operating test is independent reconstruction: an authorised reviewer should be able to determine what happened, which authority permitted the action and how the resulting business state was verified without relying on the original operator's memory. The analysis distinguishes decision custody from related concepts including accuracy, explainability, data lineage, observability and content provenance. It argues that these controls answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable forms of transparency. Content provenance might identify the history of a digital asset, for example, while providing no evidence that a user held authority to approve a payment or that the resulting transaction was correctly executed. The paper proposes eight linked evidence domains for consequential AI-influenced decisions: information received, intelligence used, rules applied, tools invoked, state changed, authority held, outcome approved and evidence preserved. These domains connect through a shared decision identifier and are intended to preserve relationships between initial inputs, policy evaluation, delegated authority, approval, execution and verified outcome. Particular attention is given to the moment of commitment, when an AI-generated recommendation becomes an external or financial business action. The paper argues that approvals must remain linked to the material terms ultimately executed. Changes to amount, recipient, purpose or other material conditions require a defined re-evaluation path rather than reliance on an earlier approval. The paper also addresses delegation across multiple agents and systems, retry behaviour, transaction reconciliation, evidence integrity, retention, human oversight and supplier evidence obligations. It distinguishes reconstruction from reproduction and outcome verification, noting that exact reproduction of stochastic model output is neither always possible nor necessary for reconstructing observable system behaviour. Three cases illustrate different dimensions of the argument. IBM provides company-reported evidence of reduced data-clearance processing time within an integrated governance programme. HSBC demonstrates large-scale financial-crime detection alongside explainable and auditable investigative outputs. AstraZeneca provides published evidence concerning the organisational scope and challenges of ethics-based AI auditing. None of these cases is presented as proof of a complete decision-custody architecture. The paper proposes consequence-based evidence requirements, independent reconstruction tests, explicit stop conditions for missing authority or mandatory evidence, supplier acceptance tests and measurable indicators including reconstruction pass rate, authority coverage, approval match, outcome reconciliation and preservation verification. The chapter concludes that auditability after an AI-influenced decision is becoming as important as intelligence before the decision. Enterprises expanding autonomous authority should first demonstrate that completed consequential decisions can be independently reconstructed from preserved evidence with clear ownership, valid authority and verified outcomes. The eight-domain decision record, consequence-based evidence model, reconstruction tests and associated management controls are author-developed conceptual frameworks informed by established provenance, AI governance, legal and assurance sources. They are not externally validated standards or universal legal requirements.

Content provenance might identify the history of a digital asset, for example, while providing no evidence that a user held authority to approve a payment or that the resulting transaction was correctly executed. The paper proposes eight linked evidence domains for consequential AI-influenced decisions: information received, intelligence used, rules applied, tools invoked, state changed, authority held, outcome approved and evidence preserved. These domains connect through a shared decision identifier and are intended to preserve relationships between initial inputs, policy evaluation, delegated authority, approval, execution and verified outcome. Particular attention is given to the moment of commitment, when an AI-generated recommendation becomes an external or financial business action. The paper argues that approvals must remain linked to the material terms ultimately executed. Changes to amount, recipient, purpose or other material conditions require a defined re-evaluation path rather than reliance on an earlier approval. The paper also addresses delegation across multiple agents and systems, retry behaviour, transaction reconciliation, evidence integrity, retention, human oversight and supplier evidence obligations. It distinguishes reconstruction from reproduction and outcome verification, noting that exact reproduction of stochastic model output is neither always possible nor necessary for reconstructing observable system behaviour. Three cases illustrate different dimensions of the argument. IBM provides company-reported evidence of reduced data-clearance processing time within an integrated governance programme. HSBC demonstrates large-scale financial-crime detection alongside explainable and auditable investigative outputs. AstraZeneca provides published evidence concerning the organisational scope and challenges of ethics-based AI auditing. None of these cases is presented as proof of a complete decision-custody architecture. The paper proposes consequence-based evidence requirements, independent reconstruction tests, explicit stop conditions for missing authority or mandatory evidence, supplier acceptance tests and measurable indicators including reconstruction pass rate, authority coverage, approval match, outcome reconciliation and preservation verification. The chapter concludes that auditability after an AI-influenced decision is becoming as important as intelligence before the decision. Enterprises expanding autonomous authority should first demonstrate that completed consequential decisions can be independently reconstructed from preserved evidence with clear ownership, valid authority and verified outcomes. The eight-domain decision record, consequence-based evidence model, reconstruction tests and associated management controls are author-developed conceptual frameworks informed by established provenance, AI governance, legal and assurance sources. They are not externally validated standards or universal legal requirements.

summary: Data and analysis code: parental care and mate desertion in the European honey buzzard Associated study Rebollo, S., Díaz-Aranda, L. M., Fernández-Pereira, J. M. & Martín-Ávila, J. A. Parental care and mate desertion in raptors: the case of the European honey buzzard, Pernis apivorus. Accepted manuscript, Animal Behaviour (manuscript 25-00749R3). This deposit provides selected processed, pseudonymized analytical datasets and R scripts associated with the study. It is not a fully validated, end-to-end reproduction package for every result in the accepted manuscript; the scope and limitations are documented below. Repository contents `data/processed/feeding_events_anonymized.csv`: chick feeding observations (assisted versus unassisted), with age, chick order and prey category. Prey categories can overlap; do not treat the full file as a single set of independent events. `data/processed/behaviour_by_nest_phase_anonymized.csv`: nest-level male and female behavioural counts or photographic time proxies, by activity and breeding phase. Not all activities have the same measurement unit. `data/processed/accelerometer_summary_anonymized.csv`: available aggregated accelerometer-derived time summaries; these do not replace the underlying time series. `data/processed/TimingOfLastPreyDelivery_anonymized.csv` and `TimingOfParentalDesertion_anonymized.csv`: paired observations for the timing of the last prey delivery and last nest activity. `data/processed/figure1_male_to_nest_distances.csv`: 217 female prey-delivery events, matched to male-to-nest distances in metres, across five pseudonymized nests. Of these, 58/217 (26.7%) fall below the 857.6 m threshold used in the manuscript. `data/summary/`: transcribed counts from Supplementary Table S8, migration-age arrays obtained from earlier R code, and a historical summary of feeding-transition models. `scripts/reproduction/`: R scripts for selected data checks, statistical analyses and figures. `documentation/`: data dictionaries, checks and known issues. `run_all.R`: runs the available reproduction scripts and reports errors; it does not certify equivalence with all published results. Running the scripts Use R with the packages required by the individual scripts, including `ggplot2` and `lme4`. From the extracted repository's root folder run: ```sh Rscript run_all.R ``` To recreate a version of Figure 1 from the deposited distances: ```sh Rscript scripts/reproduction/03_figure1_kde.R ``` Outputs, where generated, are written to `outputs/`. The scripts were assembled from available source materials but have not been validated by a complete run against the final manuscript. Scope and limitations The Figure 1 distance dataset reproduces the reported 26.7% within 857.6 m. However, time-offset summary statistics derived from this dataset differ from those printed in Supplementary Text S1; the original input/filtering should be checked before interpreting this discrepancy. Pearson chi-square calculations from the printed categories in Supplementary Table S8 yield different chi-square statistics from those in the accepted manuscript, although the conclusions about statistical significance remain unchanged. This discrepancy is documented in `documentation/KNOWN_ISSUES.md` and is not silently corrected in the archived data. The provided scripts do not reproduce every interaction test and bootstrap confidence interval reported for feeding-transition models. The complete GPS/accelerometer time series and raw nest-camera photographs are not deposited. Aggregated time-allocation data do not provide a full reproduction of all incubation analyses. The migration permutation script is included for transparency; its tail direction should be checked against the intended hypothesis before interpreting it as a two-sided test. summary: A negative and methodological result on Edward Elgar's Dorabella cipher (87 arc symbols, 14 July 1897). Thirty decipherment hypotheses were each tested against shuffled-symbol nulls and enciphered-English controls; all were ruled out or disfavoured. About 10% drawing slips reduce a standard substitution solver from 97% to about 57% accuracy on 87-letter controls, so earlier "not English" verdicts do not cover a carelessly drawn cipher; a slip-tolerant solver places Dorabella above all shuffles but below all English controls. Neighbouring arcs that are 180° flips of each other are strongly over-represented (27 of 86 against 12.6 expected, p ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁵). The cipher is not solved. title: Elgar's Dorabella cipher (14 July 1897): thirty hypothesis tests with shuffled and enciphered controls, a slip-tolerance loophole, and an excess of opposed neighbouring arcs

summary: A negative and methodological result on Edward Elgar's Dorabella cipher (87 arc symbols, 14 July 1897). Thirty decipherment hypotheses were each tested against shuffled-symbol nulls and enciphered-English controls; all were ruled out or disfavoured. About 10% drawing slips reduce a standard substitution solver from 97% to about 57% accuracy on 87-letter controls, so earlier "not English" verdicts do not cover a carelessly drawn cipher; a slip-tolerant solver places Dorabella above all shuffles but below all English controls. Neighbouring arcs that are 180° flips of each other are strongly over-represented (27 of 86 against 12.6 expected, p ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁵). The cipher is not solved. summary: RSE-AS: Research Code, Trained SAC Models, and Evaluation Results for Renewable Microgrid Energy Management This repository accompanies the research study entitled “Causality-Aware Economic Action Selection for Battery-Constrained Microgrid Energy Management: A Computational Trade-off Between Soft Actor-Critic and Model Predictive Control.” It provides the original research code, five pretrained Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) models, experimental evaluation results, and additional numerical verification artifacts for Causality-Aware Risk-Sensitive Economic Action Selection (RSE-AS) . RSE-AS is a post-policy economic action-selection mechanism that evaluates battery-feasible candidate actions using chronologically available forecasts, economic scoring, and uncertainty-dependent regularization without retraining the underlying SAC policies. Repository Contents Original research archive (Version 1) Research notebooks: Two Google Colab notebooks documenting the research workflow and dataset preparation. Pretrained SAC models: Five saved policies corresponding to random seeds 42, 43, 44, 45, and 46, each trained for 100,000 environment interactions. Chronological evaluation: Results for validation in 2021, full-year testing in 2022, and the available 8,753 hourly observations from 2023. Distribution-shift evaluation: Results under increased electricity demand (+20%), reduced photovoltaic (PV) generation (−30%), increased electricity tariffs (+50%), and combined perturbations. Ablation analysis: Comparisons among RSE-AS, Economic-Only, Fixed attenuation, Adaptive attenuation, and unmodified SAC actions. Statistical analysis: Seed-level results, paired cost differences, nominal confidence intervals, and exact two-sided sign tests. Documentation: README, software requirements, reproducibility notes, data-source attribution, and licensing information. Additional verification archive (Version 2) reproduce_rse_2023.py — Python source code for the numerical replay audit. RSE_AS_2023_hourly_all_seeds.csv — Hourly replay trajectories for five frozen SAC policies. replay_vs_original.csv — Comparison of replayed and previously recorded results. verification_report.csv — Results of the 16 implemented verification checks. verification_metadata.json — Evaluation configuration, numerical discrepancies, and software environment information. README_VERIFICATION.md — Documentation of the additional audit and its limitations. The Version 2 verification materials are included in RSE_AS_2023_Verification_Update.zip , alongside the retained original research archive. Experimental Configuration The investigated grid-connected microgrid includes a battery energy storage system with the following parameters: Nominal battery capacity: 200 kWh . Maximum charging/discharging power: 50 kW . State-of-charge (SOC) limits: 20%–90% . Charging and discharging efficiencies: 95% . Nominal initial SOC: 50% . Dispatch interval: 1 hour . SAC observation dimension: 12 . SAC action dimension: 1 . The SAC policies were trained using the 2017–2020 dataset, with 2021 reserved for validation and controller development. The complete 2022 period was used for primary chronological testing, while the available 2023 observations provided an additional evaluation period. The 2023 data were examined during research development and are not presented as a previously untouched holdout. Key Research Results Chronological economic performance During the primary 2022 test, RSE-AS achieved a mean SOC-adjusted operating cost of USD 40,954.93 , compared with USD 41,760.10 for Fixed attenuation, representing a saving of USD 805.17 (1.93%) across five pretrained SAC policies. Under four controlled distribution-shift scenarios, cost savings relative to Fixed attenuation ranged from 1.46% to 1.76% . summary: Version 1.14.0 (2026-11-14) replaces the height increment rule with a fitted height increment equation (the rule is kept as the fallback) and adds a crown base equation, a comparison with stand-level mortality forms (none adopted), and two long-term assessment metrics, with their scripts, logs and the rules written before fitting, in final_equations_20261114.zip , and supplement v127. The height, maximum stand density, diameter increment and mortality equations of version 1.13.1 are unchanged; projected height and assumed volume changed. Version 1.13.1 (2026-11-13) adds five checks of the relative-density system (benchmark with every equation refitted without the plot's installation fold, joint bootstrap of installations, the mortality equation under three death rules, benchmark after thinning, and equation S1 without the 53 Kap plots) with their scripts, logs and the inputs the scripts read, in final_equations_20261113.zip , and supplement v125. The equations and coefficients of version 1.13.0 are unchanged. Version 1.13.0 (11 November 2026) adds an annual individual-tree growth and mortality system for Acacia koa A. Gray ( koa_step_rdbyi.R and koa_rdbyi_equations.csv , both inside final_equations_20261111.zip ) that supersedes the v105final engine. An audit found that the v105final engine applies calibration multipliers, a height blend and a self-thinning step that the earlier supplement does not describe; see README.md. The new system applies the fitted equations as estimated. Diameter increment and mortality depend on relative density, the stand density index of live koa over a maximum that is predicted from the Biomass Yield Index and origin or supplied by the user. Mortality intervals that end in or span a thinning removal year of a PSP installation are censored, because the PSP database records thinned stems as dead. The rule written before the test did not prefer a maximum that varies with the Biomass Yield Index over a single value; it was adopted for consistency between fitting and use, and the README reports every test, including those that fail. No volume equation is fitted and carbon is not computed. The supplement PDF in this version is supplement v124, which describes this system. All other files are unchanged. summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Thirty-six entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten, a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation, a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight, and a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963), converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the wave-induced light fluctuations measured by Darecki et al. (2011) and Gernez & Antoine (2009), read from their figures, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters, gives the absorbance template of a visual pigment of Govardovskii et al. (2000) for a peak wavelength and chromophore the caller states, and gives the distance between two colours in units of receptor noise by the model of Vorobyev & Osorio (1998), for a noise the caller states. Without a water type, it gives Kd from the chlorophyll concentration of case 1 water (Morel & Maritorena 2001) or from the absorption and backscattering coefficients and the sun (Lee et al. 2005, 2013), the remote sensing reflectance from a and bb (Gordon et al. 1988; Lee et al. 2002), and the Secchi depth from Kd and that reflectance (Lee et al. 2015), and inverts the reflectance to the absorption and backscattering coefficients by the quasi-analytical algorithm, in the version of IOCCG Report 5 (2006), checked against that report's published statistics, and as QAA_v6, checked against its author's spreadsheet. It carries four published spectra of the absorption of pure water, Pope & Fry (1997), Smith & Baker (1981), Mason, Cone & Fry (2016) and Lee et al. (2015), for the caller to choose from, and

summary: The rapid growth of blockchain networks has raised concerns about their environmental sustainability, yet existing assessments are fragmented and often rely on problematic metrics or unverifiable self-reported data. This article addresses these gaps by combining quantitative measures of annual energy consumption and carbon emissions with a qualitative assessment of sustainability initiatives. Using data from the Crypto Carbon Ratings Institute (CCRI) and corporate sustainability reports, we evaluate Bitcoin, Ethereum, Binance Chain, XRP, Cardano, Solana, Dogecoin, Polygon, and Polkadot, and benchmark their operational footprints against those of Visa and Mastercard as representatives of traditional payment systems. Results show wide variation in sustainability performance: Proof-of-Stake networks exhibit substantially lower energy use and carbon intensity than Proof-of-Work systems, while transparency and reporting practices differ significantly across projects. This research contributes to the sustainability discourse by providing one of the first systematic comparisons between blockchain networks and incumbent payment systems, identifying methodological challenges in sustainability accounting, and advancing policy recommendations for standardized reporting, third-party verification, and energy-efficient design. This is the published version of: Mabrouk, H., Paul, L., & Wild, D. (2026). Sustainability Metrics and Disclosure Alignment in Blockchain Networks. Blockchain and Cryptocurrency, 4(1), 1–9. IFSA Publishing, S. L. Originally published on 23 March 2026. summary: Data and code that reproduce every number, table and figure in the manuscript "What Do Indonesian Artificial Intelligence Courses Teach That Industry Asks For? A Multi-University Curriculum Audit That Accounts for Lecturer Disagreement" (submitted to Computer Applications in Engineering Education). The study compares 953 course learning outcomes from 71 AI-related courses at 19 Indonesian universities with 840 requirement sentences from 51 AI job postings. A multilingual sentence-embedding model (paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2) finds the closest match in both directions, and similarity is converted into the probability that a lecturer would accept the match, using judgements from four faculty validators and a lead researcher, under six judgement standards and three calibration curve shapes. Curriculum relevance, demand coverage and their harmonic mean (alignment) are reported for the corpus, universities, Bloom levels, AI-relevance tiers, courses and skills, with cluster-bootstrap intervals, size controls, cross-validation of the calibration curves and a verb-swap check. Contents: paper4_replication.zip holds the anonymised data (universities coded U01 to U19, courses C01 to C71), the expert labels (cosine similarity, labels and job-statement group only; the texts of the judged pairs are not included), one Google Colab script (code/paper4_replication.py) and a README that maps each output file to the table or figure it produces. paper4_results.zip holds the outputs of the published run, and similarity_matrix.npy the 953 x 840 cosine similarity matrix. Raw validator forms contain personal data and are not released.
